APX-000006.transcript:
Customer (James Thompson): I signed up for budget billing so my payments would be predictable, and now I've got a CA$600 catch-up bill.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Hi James Thompson, Karabo Zulu here — let me pull that up.
Customer (James Thompson): This is the third time this year my equalized amount has changed on me.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Understood. Let me pull up the account and look at the charges before I say anything.

Customer (James Thompson): If the point of this plan is predictable payments, why does it keep moving?

Agent (Karabo Zulu): The next review is in six months, and you'll get an email two weeks before it.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): To recap, everything's noted on your file, and the team will follow up with you.
Customer (James Thompson): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Customer (Linda Duncan): Someone told me I'm being moved to a different rate class because of the August rate change. Is that true?
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Hi Linda Duncan, Vusi Jacobs here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Linda Duncan): I've been on the same rate for years, why is this changing now?
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Good question, a lot of customers are asking about this one. Let me check your account.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Before I go into the account, can you confirm the service address and the account holder's name?
Customer (Linda Duncan): Yes, same address as always, and the account's under my name.
Customer (Linda Duncan): Is this the Phase 2 thing the AUC approved, or did I do something wrong on my account?
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Roughly how much gas do you use in a year, or should I look it up?
Customer (Linda Duncan): No idea. Can you look it up?
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Did you get the letter by mail or by email?
Customer (Linda Duncan): By mail, a couple of weeks ago.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Do you have any irrigation or shop meters on the same account?

Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Okay, I've got it pulled up now.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Since August 1, Rate 1 covers accounts using under 4,000 GJ a year and Rate 2 covers larger users. The AUC approved it as Phase 2 of the rate restructuring.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Your annual usage is well under that, so you stay on Rate 1. What changed is how the distribution charge is shown on the bill.
Customer (Linda Duncan): Okay. What's the actual next step here?
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Give me one more moment while I confirm the details.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): You're on Rate 1 since your annual usage is under 4,000 GJ, so the main change is the way the distribution charge is broken out on the bill — your total shouldn't move much. I've sent the AUC decision summary to your email so you have it on file.
Customer (Linda Duncan): So my total won't go up much?
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): It shouldn't. Most of this month's jump is colder weather, not the rate change.
Customer (Linda Duncan): Can I get that in writing?
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): The AUC summary and your usage figure are in your email now.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): To recap: you're staying on Rate 1, the change is mostly how the bill is laid out, and the summary is in your email.
Customer (Linda Duncan): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Agent (Zanele Radebe): The nearest crew is on another call further out. You're next in their queue.
Customer (Robert Martin): Can we wait in the car?
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Wait away from the house, not in the driveway. I'll stay on the line until they arrive.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): To recap: a crew is coming from further out, stay away from the house, and call 911 if the smell gets stronger.
Customer (Robert Martin): Alright, thank you for looking into it.

Customer (James Murray): I'm moving next week and need gas stopped at my old place and started at the new one.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Hi James Murray, Vusi Molefe here — let me pull that up.

Agent (Vusi Molefe): No problem, I can help with that.

Customer (James Murray): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (James Murray): What's the actual turnaround time between the stop and the start?
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Is the new address in one of our service areas?
Customer (James Murray): Yes, it's still in Leduc County.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Is the email on your account still current, for the confirmations?
Customer (James Murray): It's an old one. Can you change it to my new email?

Agent (Vusi Molefe): Let me take a look. I've processed the account request and confirmed the effective date against the service address change.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Alright, I can see exactly what's going on here.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): A stop and start on the same day is routine. We read the old meter on the move-out date so you only pay to that day.
Customer (James Murray): So is this actually getting fixed today?
Agent (Vusi Molefe): I've submitted the request, but a technician visit is required to activate the new address's meter and the earliest slot is a few days out — I've flagged it as a move-in priority, but I can't guarantee same-day activation.
Customer (James Murray): So I might be without gas when I move in?
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Possibly for a day or two. The new meter needs a technician to turn it on, and the earliest slot is a few days out.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): To recap, everything's noted on your file, and the team will follow up with you.
Customer (James Murray): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Thanks for bearing with me. Everything's noted on your file, and you'll hear back as I said.

APX-000293.transcript:
Customer (Jennifer Scott): Our furnace takes a few seconds to light after the fan starts. Is that a problem?
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Hi Jennifer Scott, Zanele Radebe here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Jennifer Scott): Should I have someone look at it, or is it fine to keep using?
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Happy to help with that.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Before I go into the account, can you confirm the service address and the account holder's name?
Customer (Jennifer Scott): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Jennifer Scott): Is this something I should be worried about, or is it normal?
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Do you smell gas at all right now?
Customer (Jennifer Scott): No, nothing like that.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): How old is the furnace?
Customer (Jennifer Scott): About fifteen years.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): When was it last serviced by a licensed technician?
Customer (Jennifer Scott): A couple of years ago, I think.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Let me take a look. I've walked through the standard non-emergency safety guidance and checked for any signs that needed a field visit.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Thanks for holding — I've got the full picture now.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): A few clicks or a soft whoosh before the burner lights is the igniter and the gas catching. That's normal on most furnaces.
Customer (Jennifer Scott): Okay. What's the actual next step here?
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Give me one more moment while I confirm the details.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): What you're describing is the normal ignition sequence, so there's nothing to worry about. If the sound changes, or you ever smell gas, call us straight away.
Customer (Jennifer Scott): So I don't need anything from Apex?
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Not for this. A yearly service by a licensed technician is still a good idea at fifteen years.
Customer (Jennifer Scott): And if I ever do smell gas?
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Leave the house and call our 24-hour emergency line from outside.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): To recap: the ignition sound is normal, a yearly service is worth booking, and the emergency line is there if you ever smell gas.
Customer (Jennifer Scott): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.
